description: A comparative analysis of major critical thinking frameworks, identifying where they converge (evidence of genuine core constructs), where they diverge (genuine theoretical choices), and how they map to developmental stages and other instructional models. This synthesis is the meta-level view of the CT field.

core_convergent_constructs.description: Despite originating in different disciplines, being developed by independent researchers, and using different terminologies, the major CT frameworks converge on these constructs. This convergence is treated as empirical evidence that these constructs represent genuine components of critical thinking.

constructs.description: The ability to identify, reconstruct, and evaluate the structure of arguments — claims, reasons, evidence, and the inferential connections between them.

framework_expressions.Paul-Elder: Inference element; applying standards of clarity, accuracy, and logic to reasoning chains
framework_expressions.Ennis: Analyzing arguments (Skill A.2); identifying reasons and conclusions
framework_expressions.Delphi: Analysis core skill — examining ideas, detecting and analyzing arguments
framework_expressions.Halpern: Argument Analysis skill category — recognizing conclusions, premises, missing premises
framework_expressions.Brookfield: Identifying assumptions — arguments rest on explicit and implicit premises
framework_expressions.Toulmin: The entire model — claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal
framework_expressions.Walton: Argumentation scheme analysis — reconstructing presumptive argument patterns

constructs.consensus_view: All frameworks agree that competent argument analysis is central to critical thinking. Key sub-skills: identifying claims vs. reasons; reconstructing missing premises; evaluating inferential strength; distinguishing deductive from inductive reasoning.

constructs.description: The ability to surface the explicit and implicit premises, values, and background beliefs that arguments depend upon but often do not state.

framework_expressions.Paul-Elder: Assumptions element — all reasoning rests on assumptions; intellectual virtue: checking one's own assumptions
framework_expressions.Ennis: Identifying assumptions (Skill B.2); stated and unstated assumptions
framework_expressions.Halpern: Argument analysis sub-skill — detecting missing premises and unstated assumptions
framework_expressions.Brookfield: The central activity of CT — paradigmatic, prescriptive, and causal assumptions
framework_expressions.Walton: Critical questions for argumentation schemes expose the assumptions each scheme rests on

constructs.consensus_view: Assumption identification is universally recognized as fundamental — a defining characteristic of CT across virtually all frameworks.

constructs.description: The ability to evaluate the reliability, accuracy, and relevance of sources of evidence and testimony.

framework_expressions.Paul-Elder: Information element — evaluating sources for accuracy, relevance, and bias
framework_expressions.Ennis: Judging the credibility of sources (Skill C) — a dedicated skill cluster
framework_expressions.Delphi: Evaluation sub-skill — assessing credibility of claims and sources
framework_expressions.Halpern: Verbal Reasoning skill — evaluating claims in natural language
framework_expressions.Walton: Argument from Expert Opinion and its critical questions — is the source credible? In their domain? Consistent with other experts?

constructs.consensus_view: All frameworks recognize that CT requires evaluating not just argument structure but the evidential quality of the premises — and this requires source evaluation skills.

constructs.description: The ability to recognize and genuinely understand viewpoints, frameworks, and perspectives different from one's own.

framework_expressions.Paul-Elder: Point of View element + Empathy intellectual trait; 'Reasoning from premises one disagrees with' is itself an intellectual exercise
framework_expressions.Ennis: Disposition 8: 'Try to reason from premises one disagrees with' — perspective-taking as disposition
framework_expressions.Delphi: Open-mindedness disposition — genuinely considering alternative perspectives
framework_expressions.Halpern: Implicit in argument analysis — one must understand an argument to evaluate it
framework_expressions.Brookfield: Third activity: 'Seeing things from different viewpoints'
framework_expressions.Lipman: Community of Inquiry requires genuinely engaging with others' views — caring thinking dimension

constructs.consensus_view: Perspective-taking is both a skill (reconstructing others' reasoning) and a disposition (being willing to do so genuinely). All frameworks recognize it as essential.

constructs.description: The ability to monitor, evaluate, and correct one's own reasoning processes — thinking about thinking.

framework_expressions.Paul-Elder: 7 intellectual virtues (especially intellectual humility and intellectual integrity); self-examination across all elements
framework_expressions.Ennis: Disposition 12: 'Be reflective'; Disposition 11: 'Take a position (and change when evidence warrants)'
framework_expressions.Delphi: Self-Regulation core skill — self-monitoring and self-correction; explicit metacognitive loop
framework_expressions.Halpern: Metacognitive Monitoring component — monitoring the quality and progress of one's own thinking
framework_expressions.Brookfield: Hunting paradigmatic assumptions — the deepest assumptions about one's own way of knowing
framework_expressions.King-Kitchener: Reflective Judgment Stage 7 — the reasoner monitors their own justification process

constructs.consensus_view: All frameworks converge on self-regulation/metacognition as an essential component. The Delphi report elevates it to one of six core skills; Paul-Elder embeds it in the intellectual virtues; Halpern makes it a structural component of the full framework.

constructs.description: The motivational and attitudinal component — the will to use CT skills rather than merely possessing them.

framework_expressions.Paul-Elder: 7 Intellectual Virtues — intellectual humility, autonomy, integrity, perseverance, courage, empathy, fair-mindedness
framework_expressions.Ennis: 14 CT Dispositions organized around seeking truth, being open-minded, judging well, and acting well
framework_expressions.Delphi: CCTDI 7 subscales — Truth-seeking, Open-mindedness, Analyticity, Systematicity, Self-confidence, Inquisitiveness, Maturity
framework_expressions.Halpern: Disposition component — the will to think critically
framework_expressions.Siegel: Critical Spirit — the dispositional commitment to being governed by reasons
framework_expressions.Brookfield: An orientation to hunting assumptions — CT as a stance more than a skill

constructs.consensus_view: Skills without disposition are inert. Every major framework recognizes that CT requires both competence (skills) and commitment (disposition). The CCTDI research finding that disposition predicts skill deployment better than skill predicts disposition use has significant instructional implications: develop the critical spirit, not just the analytic skills.

divergent_issues.description: Where frameworks genuinely disagree — these are real theoretical controversies, not mere terminological differences.

position_a.label: CT skills are general and transferable across domains
position_a.argument: The same logical skills (argument analysis, source evaluation, hypothesis testing) apply whether the topic is history, science, or everyday decisions. Transfer is possible with appropriate instruction.

position_b.label: CT is inherently domain-specific; there is no generic CT
position_b.argument: What counts as good evidence, a valid argument, or a credible source depends entirely on domain-specific background knowledge. You cannot evaluate scientific reasoning without knowing the science; claiming 'CT skills' ignores this.

issues.current_position: Most contemporary frameworks adopt a moderate position: generic thinking skills exist but their application requires domain knowledge. The skill may transfer; the ability to deploy it effectively in a domain requires domain competence.
issues.instructional_implication: Teach CT frameworks explicitly, but always apply them in domain-specific contexts — ideally using the student's own field of study.

position_a.label: Critical thinking is primarily a skill set — skills are what can be taught and assessed
position_a.argument: Skills are observable and teachable; dispositions are vague and hard to assess. Focus on the cognitive competencies.

position_b.label: Disposition is primary — skills without motivation to use them are useless
position_b.argument: The CCTDI research shows that willingness to think critically is the bottleneck, not skill. People who possess CT skills but lack the disposition simply don't deploy them.

issues.current_position: Both are necessary. Skills + Disposition = Effective CT. Instructionally, developing both simultaneously is more effective than focusing exclusively on either.

position_a.label: Critical thinking is a property of individuals — an individual cognitive capacity
position_a.argument: CT can be assessed and developed in individual learners; it is an individual cognitive skill set.

position_b.label: CT is fundamentally communal — it emerges in and depends on dialogical community
position_b.argument: Ideas are tested in community; self-correction happens through dialogue; the full development of CT requires community of inquiry. Individualistic CT instruction misses this essentially social dimension.

issues.current_position: Lipman's insight is that CT has both individual and communal dimensions. Assessment focuses on individuals; instruction is strengthened by community. Both apply.

position_a.label: CT can be specified as general procedures independent of content
position_a.argument: If CT were purely content-dependent, it could not be taught as a general competency at all.

position_b.label: CT requires substantive judgment — what constitutes a good argument depends on the issue
position_b.argument: The idea that any reasoning conforming to formal procedures is 'critical' misses that the procedures must themselves be applied with judgment. Procedural compliance is not sufficient.

issues.current_position: Procedures are necessary but not sufficient. They provide scaffolding; substantive judgment (developed through domain engagement) fills the scaffolding with content.

bloom_to_ct_mapping.description: Bloom's Revised Cognitive Taxonomy provides an organizing structure for the cognitive demand of CT activities. Note that critical thinking proper begins at the Analyze level — the lower levels (Remember, Understand) are preconditions but not yet CT.

levels.name: Remember
levels.example: Recall the definition of a deductive argument

levels.name: Understand
levels.ct_activity: Interpretation (Delphi) — comprehending the meaning of an argument; necessary prerequisite for CT
levels.example: Explain in your own words what this argument claims

levels.name: Apply
levels.description: Use knowledge in a new context
levels.ct_activity: Instrumental application — may or may not be CT depending on whether judgment is required
levels.example: Apply the Toulmin model to a new argument

levels.name: Analyze
levels.description: Break complex content into components; identify relationships
levels.ct_activity: Core CT activity — Argument Analysis, Assumption Identification, Source Evaluation
levels.framework_alignment: Delphi Analysis skill; Paul-Elder Elements identification; Ennis argument analysis
levels.example: Identify the implicit premises in this argument and assess whether they are warranted

levels.name: Evaluate
levels.ct_activity: Core CT activity — evaluating argument quality, evidence strength, source credibility
levels.framework_alignment: Delphi Evaluation skill; Paul-Elder Intellectual Standards application; Ennis evaluation cluster
levels.example: Assess the strength of the evidence used to support the main claim; what alternative explanations are not addressed?

levels.name: Create
levels.ct_activity: Highest CT integration — constructing well-supported novel arguments, original syntheses
levels.framework_alignment: Paul-Elder: 'Intellectual Standards' applied to original thinking; Delphi Inference; Lipman: Creative Thinking
levels.example: Construct a well-reasoned original argument defending or criticizing a complex policy proposal

developmental_to_framework_mapping.description: Different CT frameworks are differentially appropriate for different developmental stages. Mismatching instruction to developmental level produces frustration and pseudolearning.

mappings.core_epistemology: Knowledge is certain; authority provides right answers; uncertainty means ignorance
mappings.ct_challenge: Cannot engage in genuine argument evaluation because they believe right answers exist independently of reasoning
mappings.instructional_goal: Move toward recognition that some questions require genuine inquiry rather than authority retrieval; introduce the concept that evidence varies in quality
mappings.what_not_to_teach: Complex relativistic frameworks — will be assimilated into 'there is still a right answer (just contextual)'

mappings.core_epistemology: Knowledge is uncertain; all opinions are equally valid; certainty is impossible
mappings.ct_challenge: Believes evaluation is meaningless because there is no way to adjudicate between competing views
appropriate_frameworks: Toulmin model (introducing the concept of evidence-claim structure)
mappings.instructional_goal: The crucial developmental move: help learners discover that some arguments are better-supported than others, that uncertainty does not mean equality of all views
mappings.what_not_to_teach: Full Paul-Elder framework until epistemological shift is made — the intellectual standards make no sense to a Multiplist

mappings.core_epistemology: Knowledge claims can be evaluated; some are better-supported; conclusions are provisional
mappings.ct_challenge: Can now engage fully; challenge is developing the skills to do so rigorously and the dispositions to do so habitually
mappings.instructional_goal: Develop both competence (full CT skill set) and commitment (intellectual virtues and dispositions)
mappings.what_not_to_teach: N/A — all major frameworks are accessible at this stage

assessment_taxonomy.description: How different CT assessments map to the frameworks and competencies they measure.

assessments.name: Watson-Glaser Critical Thinking Appraisal
assessments.measures: Formal reasoning sub-skills: Inference, Recognition of Assumptions, Deduction, Interpretation, Evaluation of Arguments
assessments.strength: Objective scoring; established norms; widely used
assessments.limitation: Focuses on skills without assessing dispositions; does not test argument construction

assessments.name: California Critical Thinking Skills Test (CCTST)
assessments.measures: Delphi core skills — analysis, evaluation, inference, deductive reasoning, inductive reasoning
assessments.strength: Operationalizes Delphi consensus framework; solid psychometric properties
assessments.limitation: Skills-only; does not assess dispositional dimension

assessments.name: California Critical Thinking Disposition Inventory (CCTDI)
assessments.measures: 7 dispositional subscales: Truth-seeking, Open-mindedness, Analyticity, Systematicity, Self-confidence, Inquisitiveness, Maturity
assessments.strength: The only widely-used instrument focused on CT disposition rather than skill
assessments.key_finding: Disposition scores predict actual skill deployment more strongly than skill scores alone — suggesting disposition is the practical bottleneck

assessments.name: Reflective Judgment Interview (RJI)
assessments.measures: King & Kitchener's 7 developmental stages using open-ended ill-structured problems
assessments.strength: Captures developmental dimension; rich qualitative data

siegel_reasons_conception.name: Siegel's Reasons Conception of Critical Thinking
siegel_reasons_conception.key_work: Educating Reason: Rationality, Critical Thinking and Education
siegel_reasons_conception.definition: A critical thinker is 'one who is appropriately moved by reasons' — one who acts and believes on the basis of reasons, who recognizes the force of reasons, and who is committed to being governed by reasons rather than by rhetoric, manipulation, or habit.

components.description: The cognitive skills required to evaluate reasons — assess their quality, identify their logical structure, and determine whether they support the conclusions they are claimed to support
components.relation_to_other_frameworks: Maps to Delphi Analysis + Evaluation skills; Paul-Elder Inference and Intellectual Standards

components.description: The dispositional component — the commitment to being governed by reasons. A person with the critical spirit values reasoning, values epistemic autonomy, and is motivated to evaluate and follow reasons even when it is uncomfortable to do so.
components.relation_to_other_frameworks: Maps to Paul-Elder's Intellectual Virtues; Ennis's CT Dispositions; CCTDI subscales

siegel_reasons_conception.distinctive_contribution: Siegel grounds CT in a theory of rationality rather than merely listing skills or dispositions. This gives a principled account of why CT matters: rationality is a fundamental human value, and CT is the practice of taking that value seriously.
siegel_reasons_conception.dewey_connection: Siegel's 'critical spirit' closely parallels Dewey's disposition toward reflective thinking — the cultivation of openness, directness, and responsibility in inquiry.

halpern_framework.name: Halpern's Four-Component Model
halpern_framework.description: Halpern's model emphasizes transfer — the goal of CT instruction is to produce thinking skills that transfer to new domains. Her framework has four components that work together to produce transferable CT.

components.description: The attitudinal prerequisite — willingness to engage in effortful thinking, to value accuracy over comfort, to persist when answers are not obvious
The cognitive operations themselves — organized into five categories in the HCTA
Self-awareness of the quality and accuracy of one's own thinking — the monitoring loop that catches errors and regulates reasoning processes

Explicit knowledge of the cognitive structures and principles underlying good thinking — this is what enables transfer. Without knowing *why* an argument analysis technique works, students apply it only in familiar contexts.

hcta_skill_categories.description: Evaluating claims and arguments presented in ordinary language; resisting linguistic manipulation
Identifying and evaluating explicit argument structure — premises, conclusions, implicit assumptions
Scientific reasoning skills — forming testable hypotheses, identifying confirming and disconfirming evidence, avoiding confirmation bias
Probabilistic reasoning — applying base rates, understanding conditional probability, reasoning under uncertainty
Selecting among alternatives using evidence and criteria; applying reasoning to practical decisions

halpern_framework.distinctive_contribution: The emphasis on structural knowledge for transfer sets Halpern apart. Students who know that they are looking for 'the warrant' (Toulmin) or 'the unstated premise' (Ennis) can transfer this search to new domains. Students who simply practiced on examples cannot.

walton_argumentation_schemes.name: Walton's Argumentation Schemes
walton_argumentation_schemes.description: Walton identified a catalog of approximately 25 common patterns of presumptive reasoning — informal argument structures that are reasonable and common but not deductively valid. For each scheme, he identified the 'critical questions' that, if answered negatively, defeat or rebut the argument.
walton_argumentation_schemes.key_insight: Most real-world arguments are neither deductively valid nor formally inductive — they are *presumptive*: they shift the burden of proof to the respondent, who must raise objections to defeat them. The critical questions for each scheme are the systematic way to raise such objections.

major_schemes.template: Expert E says P is true; E is an expert in domain D; P is in domain D; therefore P is (presumptively) true
critical_questions: Is E a genuine expert in domain D?
Is P actually within E's domain of expertise?
Does E have a vested interest that could bias the testimony?
Is there consensus or significant disagreement among experts on P?
Is P consistent with other established knowledge in the field?
Has E provided evidence or merely asserted P?

major_schemes.template: Case A and Case B are similar in respects R1, R2, R3; Case A has property P; therefore Case B (probably) has property P
critical_questions: Are A and B genuinely similar in the relevant respects?
Is the similarity sufficient to support the conclusion?
Are there relevant differences between A and B that undermine the analogy?
Are there other cases similar to A that do *not* have property P?

major_schemes.template: A causes B; A is present; therefore B will (probably) follow
critical_questions: Is there a genuine causal relationship between A and B, or merely correlation?
Are there circumstances in which A would not produce B?
Are there other causes of B that might produce it without A?
Has the causal relationship been established by appropriate methods?

major_schemes.template: If A is true, then B would be expected; B is observed; therefore A is (presumptively) true
critical_questions: Is B a reliable indicator of A?
Are there other explanations for B besides A?
How strong is the correlation between A and B in general?

major_schemes.template: Most people believe P; therefore P is (probably) true
critical_questions: Is popular opinion a reliable guide to truth in this domain?
Are the people whose opinion is cited well-informed about P?
Is the popularity measurement accurate?
Are there domains where popular consensus is systematically unreliable?

major_schemes.template: If we do A, then consequence C will follow; C is good/bad; therefore we should/should not do A
critical_questions: Will C actually follow from A, or is this speculation?
Is C the only relevant consequence, or are there other significant consequences?
Is C as good/bad as claimed?
Are there other ways to achieve C / avoid C besides A?

walton_argumentation_schemes.ct_application: Walton's critical questions provide a structured, practical approach to argument evaluation. Instead of asking 'is this argument valid?' (which leads to premature logical analysis), the reasoner asks 'what are the critical questions for this type of argument and can they be answered satisfactorily?'

app_usage.comparison_view: This JSON is the foundation for a framework comparison feature — showing how different frameworks address the same CT construct
app_usage.curriculum_design: The developmental mapping enables adaptive instruction: assess where the learner is developmentally, then apply appropriate framework instruction
app_usage.assessment_guidance: The assessment taxonomy helps instructors choose appropriate tools for different evaluation purposes
app_usage.deeper_reading: Each section of this synthesis can link to the detailed framework JSON for full exploration
